Question #1: Run 17 / 5, 17 %% 5, and 17 %/% 5 side by side. In your own words, explain how these three results relate to each other mathematically.

   17 / 5 = 3.4
   ,17 %% 5 = 2
   ,17 %/% 5 = 3
   
  they relate in terms of specifying every result there is when doing division [quotient, remainder, and integer quotient respectively]

  - 17/5 returns a typical division of the actual quotient, 17 %% 5 returns the remainder, while 17%/% returns the quotient without its decimal

#Part B — Basic Data Types: typeof(), class(), and mode()
  x <- 42
  y <- 42L       
  z <- "42"
  w <- TRUE
  v <- 3 + 2i 

# TODO: Use typeof() to check the type of each of x, y, z, w, v

  typeof(x) = double
  typeof(y) = integer
  typeof(z) = character
  typeof(w) = logical
  typeof(v) = complex

# TODO: Use class() to check the class of each of x, y, z, w, v
 
  > class(x)
  [1] "numeric"
  > class(y)
  [1] "integer"
  > class(z)
  [1] "character"
  > class(w)
  [1] "logical"
  > class(v)
[1] "complex"

Question #3): x <- 42 and y <- 42L look almost identical, but typeof(x) and typeof(y) give different answers. Explain the difference in your own words.

    -typeof(x) returns double because numbers are treated as doubles by R         by default, while typeof(y) returns an integer because the "L" suffix in the   end is a recognized by C and R as a special marker indicating the "long" data   type.



Question #4: Is typeof() ever different from class() and from mode() for the same object? Look at your results above and explain any case where this happens (or, if you did not see one, explain what you would expect for a matrix or factor).

  > mode (x)
  [1] "numeric"
  > mode(y)
  [1] "numeric"
  > mode(z)
  [1] "character"
  > mode(w)
  [1] "logical"
  > mode(v)
  [1] "complex"

  typeof is different to class and mode, t   typeof is more specific than both.   it     returns integers as integers and double   as a double, instead of a     higher level    generalization.

Question #5: When you ran the conversion-fail chunk, R produced NA and a warning instead of stopping with an error.

Why do you think R is designed to give a warning here rather than crashing the whole script?

  -so numeric variables could never be mistakes, or at least have it so that there is a smaller chance for error. As there are no numeric value seemingly assigned to characters, though I think there may be a way to tie them to numeric values.
  Though the warning is set likely to make sure that only well-planned exceptions get to be allowed, should they be given the trouble to have a work around.
  

What are the risks of this behavior if you don’t read your warnings?
  -missing values in a data set, concatenations not turning out the way they are planned.

 # TODO: Use paste() to combine first_name and last_name into a full name

age <- 21

paste0(first_name, " ",last_name, " ", "is", " " , age, " ", "years old")

a.) so the programmer has extra reason to be careful with handling their dat
b.) so every data input is managed and implemented as designed



Question #10: Suppose a classmate writes a script that reads a column of “numbers” from a text file. The column looks numeric, but when they try sum() on it, R throws an error. Based on everything in this lab (types, typeof()/class()/mode(), conversion, warnings), write a short paragraph explaining what likely went wrong and the steps you’d take to diagnose and fix it.

  -if an error shows up some "numbers" aren't really numbers but are numbers fashioned as strings. 
  
  step 1: use typeof() on their vectors/variables
  step 2: if there are sets that are characters, use as.numeric on them
  step 3: redo the sum() process
  


Conclusion
In 3–4 sentences, summarize what you learned about how R handles different data types, and why understanding typeof()/class() and conversion functions matters before doing arithmetic or combining data.

  - R is a bit picky when it comes to data, like if phyton was a 7 year old. R is a 5 year old - so you have to be extra specific.
  typeof() and class() and conversion matters as to make sure that the data you'll be putting in the system is in the right shapes to fit in the hypothetical holes.
